```yaml
name: Checkout code and set up npm
description: Setup code checkout, npm, and Node.js
inputs:
  ref:
    description: The branch, tag or SHA to checkout
    default: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}
    required: false
  authToken:
    description: Authentication token for npm registry
    required: true
  path:
    description: Relative path under $GITHUB_WORKSPACE to find setup node files
    default: ""
    required: false
  fetch-depth:
    description: Number of commits to fetch...
    default: "1"
    required: false
runs:
  using: "composite"
  steps:
    - name: Checkout code repository
      uses: actions/checkout@...
      with:
        path: ${{ inputs.path }}
        ref: ${{ inputs.ref }}
        fetch-depth: ${{ inputs.fetch-depth }}
    - name: Inject auth into ~/.npmrc
      id: set-workspace
      run: |
        echo -e "\n//common.repositories.cloud.sap/artifactory/api/npm/…_authToken=…"
        …
      shell: bash
      env:
        BTPAI_NPM_TOKEN: ${{ inputs.authToken }}
    - name: Setup node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@...
      with:
        node-version-file: ${{ inputs.path }}/.nmrc
        cache: npm
        cache-dependency-path: ${{ inputs.path }}/package-lock.json
    - name: Install dependencies
      working-directory: ${{ inputs.path }}
      run: npm ci
      shell: bash
```

The image is a screenshot / copy-paste of an explanatory text about a macOS bash startup-file problem.

* The core point is that on macOS, bash login shells – the shells you get in Terminal.app windows – read `~/.bash_profile`, not `~/.bashrc`.  
  `Your .bash_profile never sources .bashrc, so none of the exports there — including GITHUB_TOKEN — are ever loaded.`

* The fix that is recommended is to make `.bash_profile` source `.bashrc`:
  ```
  [ -r ~/.bashrc ] && source ~/.bashrc
  ```
  The text says *Add this line to .bash_profile* and shows the resulting file as e.g.
  ```
  export PATH=~/git-gu:$PATH
  [ -r ~/.bashrc ] && source ~/.bashrc
  ```

* The author notes that the line `[ -r ~/.bashrc ] && source ~/.bashrc` was actually already present, garbled, as lines 49-50 of the user’s `.bashrc` – i.e. the instructions were pasted into the wrong file.  
  Once the sourcing line is placed in `.bash_profile`, opening a new terminal and running `echo $GITHUB_TOKEN` should work.

* A security side note is given:  
  *Side note: before you do this, you should revoke that GitHub token and replace it with a fresh one — it’s been exposed in plaintext in a file on disk, and I’ve already read it. Rotate it at github.com → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens.*

That is the visible content of the picture.

* **Search UI** – At the top is the search bar with the query “azure backup operation types”. Below it are the normal Google tabs: AI Mode, All (selected/underlined), Images, Videos, Short videos, News, Forums, More, Tools.

* **AI Overview block** – Introduced by a blue star icon and the label “AI Overview”.

  *“Azure backup operation types include full, incremental, and differential backups, which differ in how they save data changes. There are also operational types like register, configure backup, backup, restore, and disable backup, which are performed on a Recovery Services vault. In terms of data types, Azure supports backing up Azure VMs, Azure Files, SQL Server in VMs, SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Databases, Azure Blobs, and on-premises workloads via agents like MARS, DPM, or MABS.”*

* **Backup method types** – a bulleted section:
  * **Full Backup:** Backs up the entire dataset. It can be restored independently, but it is the most storage-intensive method.
  * **Incremental Backup:** Backs up only the data that has changed since the last backup, whether it was a full or incremental one. This saves storage space and is faster to create.
  * **Differential Backup:** Backs up all data that has changed since the last full backup. It consumes more storage than an incremental backup, but it can restore data faster as it only needs the last full backup and the latest differential backup.

* **Operational types** – a bulleted section:
  * **Register:** Registering a server with a Recovery Services vault.
  * **Configure backup:** Setting up the backup policy for a protected item.
  * **Backup:** Performing a backup on demand.
  * **Restore:** Restoring data from a backup.
  * **Disable backup:** Disabling the backup for a protected item.
  * **Delete backup data:** Deleting the backup data stored in the vault.

The content is a concise summary of Azure Backup operation/backup method types and the operational actions you can perform on a Recovery Services vault.
